title: Mathematical toolkit
subtitle: Tools that make the ideas precise
prerequisites: Foundations; arithmetic and basic equation rearrangement. This is an introductory bridge, not a substitute for extended calculus and linear-algebra practice.

lessons.title: Measure a turn without degrees
lessons.idea: An angle tells us how far something turns. A radian is one way to measure that turn.
body: The radius is the straight distance from a circle’s centre to its edge. The diameter goes straight across through the centre, from one edge to the opposite edge. It is two radii long.
An arc is just part of the curved edge. The whole way around is the circumference. To measure a particular turn, use the arc traced by that turn—not automatically the whole circumference.
A degree is one of 360 equal parts of a full turn. A quarter-turn is 90 degrees, written 90°. Degrees and radians measure the same turn in different units.
A turn is one radian when its arc is the same length as the radius. On a circle with a 2 cm radius, trace 2 cm along the edge: that turn is 1 radian. Trace 4 cm instead: the turn is 2 radians.

π (pi) is the circumference divided by the diameter, the same fixed number for every circle: about 3.14. A full turn traces the whole edge, which is 2π radius-lengths long. Here 2π means 2 times π, about 6.28. So a full turn is exactly 2π radians, or about 6.28 radians.
lessons.terms: θ (theta) names the turn size in radians. s is the traced arc length; r is the radius. Use the same length unit for s and r, and a radius greater than zero.

example.title: A 2 cm arc on a circle with a 2 cm radius
steps: The radius r is 2 cm. The traced arc s is also 2 cm.
Divide the curved distance by the radius: θ = 2 cm ÷ 2 cm = 1 radian.
That turn covers one radius-length along the edge. It is only part of a full turn, not the whole circumference.

visual.title: Count radius-lengths along the arc
visual.caption: Gold shows the centre-to-edge radius. Green shows the curved arc traced by the turn. Change either control: arc length equals radius × turn in radians. This is a diagram, not actual size. The slider’s 6.28 rad endpoint is close to a full turn, not exactly 2π.

check.prompt: A circle has a 3 cm radius. A turn traces a 6 cm arc. How large is the turn?
explanations: One radian would trace an arc equal to the radius: 3 cm, not 6 cm.
Yes. 6 cm ÷ 3 cm = 2. The arc contains two radius-lengths, so the turn is 2 radians.
6 cm is the arc length. Divide it by the 3 cm radius to find the angle.

apply.title: Try the relationship in reverse
apply.text: A wheel has a 4 cm radius and turns about a fixed centre through 3 radians. How far does a point on its edge travel along the curved edge?
apply.answer: One radian traces one radius-length, or 4 cm here. Three radians trace three radius-lengths: 3 × 4 cm = 12 cm of arc. This is the curved distance around the edge, not a straight line between the start and finish.

lessons.limits: This definition uses a circle with a positive radius. Arc length is measured along the curve, not across it. Use matching length units for the arc and radius. Radians and degrees are different units for the same turn. The model shows turn size, so its displayed angles are nonnegative.

equationGuide.meaning: Divide the arc length by the radius. The answer tells you how many radius-lengths fit along that arc—and that is the angle in radians.

lessons.title: Resolve an angled vector
lessons.idea: A slanted arrow can describe a move right or left and a move up or down.
body: A slanted arrow can describe a move right or left and a move up or down. These two parts are its components. Choose right as positive x and up as positive y. The two directions meet at a right angle, like the sides of a square.

Let r be the full arrow length and θ, said theta, its angle counterclockwise from right. Cosine tells us the horizontal share of the length; sine tells us the vertical share. Multiply r by each share to find x and y. Negative answers mean left or down. These are two parts of one arrow, not two distances to add into a path.
To convert a number of degrees into radians, multiply it by π/180. For 60°, this gives 60 × π/180 = π/3 rad. Match the calculator’s degree or radian mode to the angle number you enter.
lessons.equation: x = r cos θ;  y = r sin θ;  radians = degrees × π/180

example.title: An angled displacement
steps: Take r = 2 m and θ = 60°.
x = 1 m and y ≈ 1.732 m. Their squared lengths add to 4 m².

check.prompt: A 3 m vector points straight downward, at 270° from positive x. What are its components?
explanations: Yes. Down is negative y and there is no horizontal component.
That vector points right, not down.
Positive y points up under the chosen convention.

apply.title: Break a force into parts
apply.text: A 10 N force acts at 60° above horizontal. How large is the horizontal component?
apply.answer: The horizontal part is 10 × cos 60° = 5 N, where N means newtons of force. The vertical part is 10 × sin 60° ≈ 8.66 N. These are parts of the same 10 N force; adding their sizes does not give its full magnitude.

lessons.limits: These relations use perpendicular Cartesian axes and the stated angle convention. Calculator degree/radian mode must match the input.

equationGuide.meaning: Horizontal component equals length times cosine of the angle; vertical component equals length times sine. The final rule converts the numerical degree reading to a radian reading.

lessons.title: Use the signs to find the quadrant
lessons.idea: A minus sign can tell us direction rather than a negative length.
body: A minus sign can tell us direction rather than a negative length. Choose right and up as positive. Then x = −3 m means 3 metres left and y = 4 m means 4 metres up.

To find the arrow’s length, square both perpendicular components, add, then take the square root. Squaring means multiplying a number by itself. The nonnegative square root turns the summed squared lengths back into a length: √[(−3 m)² + (4 m)²] = 5 m.

The axes divide the page into four regions, called quadrants. These signs put the arrow in the upper-left region. An inverse-tangent calculation using only y/x can confuse opposite regions. The calculator function atan2(y,x) uses both signs to choose the direction. A zero-length arrow has no direction.

steps: Let x = −3 m and y = +4 m.
Magnitude = √(9 + 16) = 5 m.
The vector points left and up, so its angle lies between 90° and 180°.

check.prompt: A vector has x = −2 N and y = −2 N. Which direction quadrant contains it?
explanations: The negative x component points left.
The negative y component points down.
Yes. Both components are negative.

apply.title: Check a force answer
apply.text: A calculation gives a force magnitude of −7 N. What should you check?
apply.answer: A magnitude should be nonnegative. The negative sign may belong to a component or chosen direction, not to the magnitude. Rewrite the vector with explicit components or magnitude and direction.

lessons.limits: These sign conventions are choices, not universal labels. State the axes before interpreting components.

lessons.title: Two vector products answer different questions
lessons.idea: There are two useful ways to multiply arrows, which are called vectors.
body: There are two useful ways to multiply arrows, which are called vectors. The dot product gives one signed number showing how much they point along one another. The cross product gives an arrow showing how much they point across one another, together with an orientation.

For a·b, multiply their matching x parts, then matching y parts, then matching z parts, and add. A subscript such as aₓ labels a part; it does not mean a times x. The answer is a scalar: a number without a direction. Units multiply too: metres times metres gives square metres.

The cross-product length is |a||b| sin θ, where θ is the angle between the input arrows. To find its direction, point your right-hand fingers along a and curl them toward b; your thumb points along a×b. Reversing the input order reverses that direction. A zero cross product has no direction. For arrows in the xy plane, its z part is aₓbᵧ − aᵧbₓ.
lessons.equation: a·b = aₓbₓ + aᵧbᵧ + a_zb_z;  |a×b| = |a||b| sin θ

example.title: Alignment and area
steps: Their dot product is zero because they are perpendicular.
Their cross product is (0,0,6) m² under right-handed axes. Its magnitude is the parallelogram area.
The two input arrows meet at a right angle. They span a 2 m by 3 m rectangle, whose area is 6 m². This illustrates the cross-product magnitude.

visual.title: Two vector products answer different questions
visual.caption: For fixed input magnitudes, the angle controls dot and cross products. The dot product is scalar; the cross product uses a right-handed three-dimensional orientation.

check.prompt: A force (3,4,0) N acts through displacement (2,0,0) m. What is their dot product?
explanations: Multiply matching components, not the force magnitude by a chosen component.
The y force has no y displacement here.

apply.title: Choose the operation
apply.text: Which operation belongs in work F·Δr, and which belongs in torque r×F?
apply.answer: Work is energy transferred by a force along a displacement. F is force in newtons (N), and Δr is displacement in metres (m). For a constant force over this displacement, the dot product F·Δr gives work in joules (J), where 1 J = 1 N·m. Torque is a force’s turning effect about a chosen point. In r×F, r runs from that point to where the force acts; the cross product gives the turning direction. Torque uses N·m too, but unlike work it is a vector.

lessons.limits: For changing forces, work is a line integral. The familiar cross product used here is the three-dimensional Cartesian one.

practice.prompt: Use a = (2, −1, 0) and b = (3, 4, 0), both dimensionless.
practice.reasoning: Why can the dot product be small while the cross-product magnitude is large? They measure different geometric relations: alignment and oriented perpendicular extent.

equationGuide.meaning: The dot product adds matching component products. The cross-product magnitude multiplies both arrow lengths by the sine of their angle.

lessons.title: Ask for the rate right now
lessons.idea: A derivative tells us how quickly an output changes near one chosen input.
body: A derivative tells us how quickly an output changes near one chosen input. A car’s velocity right now describes how quickly its position is changing now, rather than its average over a whole trip.

A function is a rule from input to output. f(x) means the output when rule f receives input x. Here f(x) = x² means square x. The notation df/dx names its rate of change with x; it is one piece of notation, not ordinary division by zero. For this rule the rate is 2x. At x = 3, the output is 9 but the rate is 6.

A tangent is a straight line with the same local slope as the curve at one point. For a small input change, slope times input change estimates the output change. All numbers in the square example are dimensionless; a physical rate has output units divided by input units.

Unit key: m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton (force), J joule (energy), K kelvin (temperature), C coulomb (electric charge), and rad radian (angle). A slash means per; a dot between units multiplies them. A superscript ² means squared. A dimensionless number has no physical unit.

example.title: A local slope
steps: Choose x = 3 in f(x) = x².
The function value is 9; its derivative is 2 × 3 = 6.
A small input increase of 0.01 gives an output increase of about 6 × 0.01 = 0.06. The exact increase is 0.0601.

visual.title: Ask for the rate right now
visual.caption: The tangent is a local linear approximation to a dimensionless parabola. It is not an additional physical trajectory.

check.prompt: For f(x) = x², what is the derivative at x = 4?
explanations: 16 is the function value, not its derivative.
The rule is 2x, not x.
Yes. The derivative is 2x, giving 8.

apply.title: Velocity from position
apply.text: A cart has position x(t) = (0.5 m/s²)t². What is its velocity at t = 3 s?
apply.answer: Here x(t) names position in metres, t is time in seconds, and v is velocity. Differentiate x(t) = (0.5 m/s²)t² with respect to t: v(t) = (1 m/s²)t. At 3 s the velocity is 3 m/s. Position is increasing at that rate at that instant; this does not say the rate stays the same for the next full second.

lessons.limits: Not every function has a derivative at every point. A sharp corner can have different slopes on its two sides.

equationGuide.meaning: The function squares the input. Its derivative says how fast the output changes per small change in input.

lessons.title: Differentiate a power
lessons.idea: A power tells us how many times to multiply an input by itself: x³ means x × x × x.
body: A power tells us how many times to multiply an input by itself: x³ means x × x × x. For positive whole-number powers, the power rule finds the rate: multiply by the power, then lower that power by one. So the rate of x³ is 3x².

In d(xⁿ)/dx = n xⁿ⁻¹, n names the fixed power and d/dx asks for a rate with respect to x. A constant C does not change when x changes, so its rate is zero. You can differentiate added terms separately, and a fixed multiplier stays as a multiplier. The elementary examples use dimensionless inputs.

C: constant; A value independent of x (same units as its output). Unit key: m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton (force), J joule (energy), K kelvin (temperature), C coulomb (electric charge), and rad radian (angle). A slash means per; a dot between units multiplies them. A superscript ² means squared. A dimensionless number has no physical unit.

example.title: A cubic model
steps: Let f(x) = 2x³ − 5.
Differentiate term by term: df/dx = 6x².
At x = 2, the local slope is 24. The original function value is 11.

visual.title: Differentiate a power
visual.caption: A function value and its derivative are different outputs. This numerical example is dimensionless.

check.prompt: What is d(3x² + 8)/dx?
explanations: Yes. The derivative of 3x² is 6x and the constant contributes zero.
The exponent 2 must multiply the coefficient.
The added constant does not change when x changes.

apply.title: From position to acceleration
apply.text: A model has x(t) = At³, where A = 0.2 m/s³. Find acceleration at t = 2 s.
apply.answer: x is position, t is time, and A = 0.2 m/s³ is a constant multiplier chosen so At³ has units of metres. First take the time derivative to get velocity v = 3At². Differentiate again to get acceleration a = 6At. At t = 2 s, a = 6 × 0.2 × 2 = 2.4 m/s². Each time derivative changes the units to the previous units per second.

lessons.limits: Fractional and negative powers require attention to the real domain and singular points. This rule does not differentiate x raised to a variable exponent without further work.

equationGuide.meaning: Multiply a power expression by its exponent and reduce the exponent by one to get its derivative on the domain where this rule applies. A constant has zero derivative.

lessons.title: Differentiate a product carefully
lessons.idea: When two changing quantities are multiplied, either one can change the result.
body: When two changing quantities are multiplied, either one can change the result. The derivative therefore needs two parts, not just the product of their two derivatives.

Let f and g both depend on x. First multiply f’s rate by g’s current value. Then add f’s current value times g’s rate. That is d(fg)/dx = (df/dx)g + f(dg/dx). A prime, such as f′, means the same derivative here.

Unit key: m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton (force), J joule (energy), K kelvin (temperature), C coulomb (electric charge), and rad radian (angle). A slash means per; a dot between units multiplies them. A superscript ² means squared. A dimensionless number has no physical unit.

example.title: Two growing factors
steps: Take f = x² and g = x³.
The product rule gives 2x·x³ + x²·3x² = 5x⁴.
Check by multiplying first: fg = x⁵, whose derivative is also 5x⁴.

check.prompt: For h(x) = x(x + 2), what is h′(x)?
explanations: That multiplies the derivatives and misses the product rule.
That includes only one contribution.

apply.title: Differentiate kinetic energy
apply.text: For constant mass m, K = ½mv² and v depends on time. Why is dK/dt = mv(dv/dt)?
apply.answer: K is kinetic energy in joules, m is constant mass in kilograms and v is speed in m/s. Write v² as v·v. The two product-rule contributions are (dv/dt)v and v(dv/dt), so they add to 2v(dv/dt). Multiplying by ½m cancels that 2, leaving dK/dt = mv(dv/dt). The dot notation v̇ also means dv/dt, an acceleration in m/s². dK/dt is an energy-transfer rate in J/s.

lessons.limits: If mass also changes with time, its derivative contributes too. Do not silently hold a changing physical quantity constant.

equationGuide.meaning: The rate of a product is the first factor’s rate times the second factor, plus the first factor times the second factor’s rate.

lessons.title: Differentiate an inside–outside relationship
lessons.idea: Sometimes a change passes through two linked steps.
body: Sometimes a change passes through two linked steps. The first input changes a middle value, and that middle value changes the final output. Multiply the two rates to find the overall rate.

Call the first input x, the middle value u and the output y. If y = u², its rate with u is 2u. If u = 3x, its rate with x is 3. Multiplying gives dy/dx = 6u = 18x. At x = 1 that is a slope of 18; it is not a statement that the output y equals 18.

Unit key: m means metre, s second, kg kilogram, N newton (force), J joule (energy), K kelvin (temperature), C coulomb (electric charge), and rad radian (angle). A slash means per; a dot between units multiplies them. A superscript ² means squared. A dimensionless number has no physical unit.

steps: Let y = (2x + 1)².
Outside derivative: 2(2x+1). Inside derivative: 2.
Multiply to obtain dy/dx = 4(2x+1). At x = 1, the slope is 12.

check.prompt: What is d((5x)²)/dx?
explanations: 25 is the coefficient of x² before differentiating.
That omits one factor of 5 from the inner derivative.

apply.title: Track an inner rate
apply.text: A dimensionless function is y(t) = [2(t/s) + 1]³. What is dy/dt at t = 0? Here t is time and s denotes one second.
apply.answer: In this question, t/s means t divided by one second, so it is a unit-free time number. Set u = 2[t/(1 s)] + 1. The outer rate of u³ is 3u²; the inner time rate is 2 s⁻¹, meaning 2 per second. Their product is 6u² s⁻¹. At t = 0, u = 1, so dy/dt = 6 s⁻¹: the dimensionless output changes at a rate of 6 per second.

lessons.limits: The inner and outer functions must be differentiable at the relevant values. For multiple changing inputs, use the multivariable chain rule.

equationGuide.meaning: Overall output change per input change equals output change per middle-value change times middle-value change per input change.

lessons.title: Use a small set of basic rates
lessons.idea: Sine and cosine repeat like smooth waves.
body: Sine and cosine repeat like smooth waves. Their rate rules are linked: sine’s rate is cosine, while cosine’s rate is minus sine. These rules use radian input. A prime mark, ′, means rate of change with the input.

The number e is fixed, about 2.71828. The exponential eˣ has a special property: its rate equals its current value. A linked input still needs the chain rule. For e^(−kt), multiply the outer rate e^(−kt) by the inner rate −k. A positive k makes this a decreasing exponential.

steps: Let q(t) = 5e^(−2t), with t dimensionless for this example.

apply.title: Verify a restoring acceleration
apply.text: For x(t) = A cos(ωt), differentiate twice.
apply.answer: A is the largest displacement from the centre in metres, ω is angle-change rate in rad/s, and t is time in seconds. x(t) is position. Its first time derivative is velocity v = −Aω sin(ωt), in m/s. Differentiate again to get acceleration a = −Aω² cos(ωt) = −ω²x, in m/s². This says acceleration points toward the centre and grows in size with distance from it. This repeating motion is called simple harmonic motion.

lessons.title: Add tiny contributions
lessons.idea: An integral adds many small pieces to find a total.
body: An integral adds many small pieces to find a total. If velocity changes during a trip, split the time into short parts and add the displacement from each part instead of pretending one velocity lasted throughout.

The sign ∫ means add continuously. In ∫ₐᵇ 2x dx, a is the start input, b is the end input, and dx says the sum is over x. Since x² has rate 2x, the total is b² − a². From 0 to 3 that is 9 in this unit-free example.

Positive and negative contributions keep their signs. A velocity–time area gives displacement: negative velocity subtracts. Total distance instead counts every travelled piece positively. To find final position, add displacement to the starting position.

steps: Let velocity v(t) = (2 m/s²)t from t = 0 to 3 s.
The velocity–time area is a triangle: ½ × 3 s × 6 m/s.
Displacement = 9 m. The integral gives the same result.
The triangle is 3 s wide and 6 m/s high. Multiplying seconds by metres per second gives metres. Its 9 m area is a displacement, not a velocity.

check.prompt: A flow rate is 2 litres/min for 4 minutes. What does its time integral give?

Yes. Rate × duration has units of volume.
That divides rate by time; accumulation multiplies by time.

apply.text: If velocity is known over a time interval, does its integral alone give final position?
apply.answer: It gives displacement. Add the initial position to obtain final position. Integration needs the appropriate starting information.

lessons.title: Recover a family, not one answer
lessons.idea: Knowing a rate does not tell us where something started.
body: Knowing a rate does not tell us where something started. Two cars can have the same velocity but start at different positions. An antiderivative is a rule whose derivative gives the rate we started with.

For a power xⁿ, raise the power by one, divide by that new power, and add C. For x², the result is x³/3 + C. C is any constant offset because a constant’s derivative is zero. This formula excludes n = −1, where its denominator would be zero.

An integral written without start and end limits returns a family of functions, not a numerical total. A given value at a particular input fixes C. For a physical quantity, C has the same units as the result; it is not necessarily a unit-free number.

steps: Acceleration is a = 3 m/s², constant.
Integrate in time: v(t) = (3 m/s²)t + C.
If v(0) = 2 m/s, then C = 2 m/s.
Here v(t) = (3 m/s²)t + 2 m/s starts at 2 m/s and gains 3 m/s each second. The constant has velocity units, just like the whole result.

Its derivative is 16x³, four times too large.
Yes. Differentiating x⁴ returns 4x³; C disappears.

apply.title: Why two initial conditions?
apply.text: To recover position from a known acceleration function, why do you generally need two pieces of initial data?
apply.answer: Integrating acceleration gives velocity plus one constant. Integrating velocity gives position plus another. Initial velocity and initial position fix the two constants.

lessons.idea: To find a total between two inputs, find an antiderivative and subtract its starting value from its ending value.

In ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), a says where to start and b says where to end. F(b) means put b into the antiderivative; F(a) means put a into it. Subtract in that order. Reversing the endpoints reverses the signed total.

steps: Find ∫ from 1 to 3 of 2x dx.
An antiderivative is x².
Evaluate 3² − 1² = 9 − 1 = 8.
The inputs 1 and 3 and the output here are dimensionless. The result 8 is the total accumulation, not the value of 2x at either endpoint.

explanations: The endpoints differ; reversing them does not erase the accumulated value.
Yes. Reversing the limits reverses the sign.
The ordering of the limits matters.

apply.title: A variable force
apply.text: A force F(x) = kx acts along the displacement from x = 0 to L. What is its work?
apply.answer: Here F is a force, not the capital-F antiderivative used above. k in N/m says how much the force increases per metre, x is position in m, and L is the ending position. Work W is energy transferred by force along motion, in J. Add force times displacement: W = ∫₀ᴸ kx dx = ½kL². For example, k = 2 N/m and L = 3 m give 9 J. The expression F = kx is the stated applied force; it is not automatically the restoring spring force −kx. Signs depend on the given force and direction.

lessons.limits: For work, use the force component along the path. A scalar area formula alone is not enough for an arbitrary three-dimensional path.

lessons.title: Recognize a hidden inside variable
lessons.idea: A repeated expression can be given a short temporary name.
body: A repeated expression can be given a short temporary name. This can turn an integral into a simpler one. The expression being integrated is called the integrand.

For ∫2x cos(x²) dx, name x² as u. Its rate is 2x, so du = 2x dx replaces that whole part of the integral. Now integrate cos u to get sin u + C. Replace u with x² again: sin(x²) + C. The inputs here have no physical units, and angles are in radians.

With start and end limits, convert those limits to the new variable too. The bounds and the integrand must use the same input. After changing variables in the example, the total e − 1 ≈ 1.718 is an accumulated value, not a slope.

lessons.title: Reverse the product rule
lessons.idea: An integral of a product is sometimes easier if we swap which factor we differentiate and which we integrate.
body: An integral of a product is sometimes easier if we swap which factor we differentiate and which we integrate. This method comes from the product rule for derivatives.

Choose one part as u and the other as dv. Then du is u’s derivative times the input step, and v is an antiderivative of the part in dv. The rule is ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. For x eˣ, choose u = x and dv = eˣ dx; this gives du = dx and v = eˣ.

With endpoints a and b, replace uv by its end value minus its start value: [uv]ₐᵇ = u(b)v(b) − u(a)v(a). Then subtract the remaining integral over the same interval. These endpoint values are sometimes called boundary terms. The examples here use dimensionless inputs and outputs.

steps: Find ∫ x eˣ dx. Choose u = x and dv = eˣ dx.
Then du = dx and v = eˣ.
The result is x eˣ − eˣ + C = (x − 1)eˣ + C.
The final function (x − 1)eˣ + C has derivative x eˣ. It is an antiderivative, not the original integrand.

You need an antiderivative of cos x, not the same function.
Yes. An antiderivative of cos x is sin x.

apply.title: Finish and check
apply.text: Using that choice, what is ∫ x cos x dx?
apply.answer: For ∫x cos x dx, choose u = x and dv = cos x dx. Then du = dx and v = sin x. The rule gives x sin x − ∫sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + C. Check by differentiating: sin x + x cos x − sin x = x cos x. Here x is dimensionless and trigonometric inputs are radians.

lessons.title: Hold the other inputs fixed
lessons.idea: A room can be warmer farther east and warmer farther north.
body: A room can be warmer farther east and warmer farther north. To ask only about the eastward change, hold the north–south position fixed. A partial derivative changes one input at a time while the other independent inputs stay fixed.

For f(x,y) = x² + 3y, the curled symbol ∂ marks a partial derivative. ∂f/∂x changes x while keeping y fixed, giving 2x. ∂f/∂y instead changes y while keeping x fixed, giving 3. At (2,1), the output is 7, but the two rates are 4 and 3. They answer different questions.

lessons.title: Track several changing inputs
lessons.idea: If a rectangle gets both longer and wider, both changes affect its area.
body: If a rectangle gets both longer and wider, both changes affect its area. To find its rate of area change, count each input’s contribution and add them.

Let f depend on x and y, which both change with time t. fₓ means the rate of f with x while y stays fixed; fᵧ means the rate with y while x stays fixed. Multiply fₓ by x’s time rate dx/dt, and fᵧ by y’s time rate dy/dt. Their sum is df/dt.

This rate equation is exact when f is differentiable, x(t) and y(t) have derivatives, and f has no separate time dependence. Differentiable means the function has a consistent local linear approximation, not just separate coordinate rates. For small finite changes instead, Δf ≈ fₓΔx + fᵧΔy is an estimate. The triangle-shaped Δ means a finite change; it is not interchangeable with the derivative notation d.

The x growth contributes y × dx/dt = 0.3 m²/s; the y growth contributes x × dy/dt = 0.4 m²/s. Together the area is growing at 0.7 m²/s at this instant.

apply.title: Follow a moving sensor
apply.text: A sensor moves through a time-independent temperature field T(x,y). Can its measured temperature change with time?
apply.answer: Yes. T is temperature in kelvins, x and y are position coordinates in metres, and vₓ and vᵧ are the sensor’s velocity components in m/s. Multiply each spatial temperature rate in K/m by its velocity component and add: dT/dt = (∂T/∂x)vₓ + (∂T/∂y)vᵧ. This gives K/s. If the field itself also changes with time, add its local time rate ∂T/∂t; the stated question excludes that extra change.

lessons.title: Collect the directions of local change
lessons.idea: Imagine a temperature map.
body: Imagine a temperature map. At a spot where temperature changes with position, the gradient is an arrow pointing toward the fastest local increase. Its length gives how much the value increases per unit distance in that direction.

The notation ∇f means the gradient of f. It collects the separate rates along perpendicular coordinate directions. A small move Δr produces an estimated change Δf ≈ ∇f·Δr: multiply matching components and add. The ≈ sign warns that this is only a local estimate for a finite move.

The exact differential df = ∇f·dr describes the linear rate relation itself. It is not a promise that a finite change equals that linear estimate. A contour is a line of equal values. Where the gradient is nonzero, it is perpendicular to a smooth contour because moving along that contour gives no local increase.

A small displacement (0.01,0) gives predicted change 0.02.

Positive x gives a positive first-order change.
Negative x gives a negative first-order change.

apply.title: Read a contour line
apply.text: Why is a gradient perpendicular to a smooth constant-value contour?
apply.answer: A contour is a line on which f keeps the same value. Its tangent points along the line at one spot. The local slope-based change in that direction is zero, so the tangent has zero dot product with the gradient. A nonzero gradient must therefore be perpendicular to that tangent. A zero gradient has no direction.

lessons.limits: At a critical point where the gradient vanishes, higher-order changes matter. In non-Cartesian coordinates, gradient components include coordinate scale factors.

lessons.title: Use a nearby simple model
lessons.idea: Near one point, a smooth curve can look almost straight.
body: Near one point, a smooth curve can look almost straight. Use its value and slope there to estimate a nearby value without calculating the whole rule again.

Let x₀ be the starting input and Δx a small input change. The estimate says: new output ≈ old output + slope × input change. f(x₀) is the old output and f′(x₀) is its slope. The prime means derivative; the small zero labels the reference input.

The error from this straight-line estimate is not automatically a measurement uncertainty. In the square example, the exact answer is 9.61 and the estimate is 9.6: the missing 0.01 comes from the curve, not from imperfect measuring. Larger steps may make the estimate poor.

apply.text: A measured positive length L has a small uncertainty δL. For area A = L², what first-order uncertainty scale follows?

These are local estimates, not guaranteed error bounds or confidence levels.

lessons.title: Give every position a value
lessons.idea: A field is a rule that gives a value at each place.
body: A field is a rule that gives a value at each place. A temperature map gives one number at each place: a scalar field. A wind map gives a speed and direction: a vector field. A field is not itself the path followed by an object.

For a scalar field f, the gradient ∇f collects its local change rates into an arrow. In two perpendicular directions it is (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y). The first part describes an x-direction change with y held fixed; the second describes a y-direction change with x held fixed. For temperature measured in kelvins and position in metres, both rates have units K/m.

apply.text: If electric potential decreases most rapidly toward the right, which way does the electric field point?
apply.answer: In electrostatics, where the relevant electric field is time-independent, it points right in this example. V names electric potential, an energy-per-charge quantity measured in volts. E names electric field. E = −∇V says the field points toward decreasing potential, opposite the gradient. Volts per metre (V/m) equal newtons per coulomb (N/C). This relation by itself does not describe arbitrary time-changing electromagnetic fields.

lessons.title: Add along a path
lessons.idea: A force transfers energy when the point it acts on moves along its direction.
body: A force transfers energy when the point it acts on moves along its direction. That energy transfer is called work. On a curved path, the direction of travel may change. Split the trip into tiny directed moves and add the work from each one.

In W = ∫path F·dr, F is force and dr is a tiny displacement along the path. The dot product selects the force part along that move. The integral adds these contributions over the chosen route. A force perpendicular to a move gives zero work on that part, even though the force is still present.

The direction in which you follow the route is its orientation. Reversing the same route in a fixed field reverses the work’s sign. A conservative field is a special case whose work depends only on start and end points; that does not follow just from being able to reverse a path.

Total work is 8 J, despite a path length of 5 m.
The 3 m upward segment still has a 4 N rightward force, but those directions are perpendicular. Its contribution is zero, so only the first 2 m segment supplies the 8 J total.

apply.answer: It changes sign because every oriented displacement dr reverses. This does not by itself say the field is conservative.

lessons.title: Count the part passing through a surface
lessons.idea: Flux measures how strongly a field points through a surface, counting the surface area too.
body: Flux measures how strongly a field points through a surface, counting the surface area too. A field pointing along a sheet contributes no through-sheet flux. This need not be a material flow: electric flux is a mathematical measure of an electric field.

Imagine an arrow sticking straight out of the sheet. This is its normal, meaning perpendicular direction. The angle θ is between this normal and the field, not between the field and the sheet. For a flat area A in a uniform field of size E, Φ = EA cos θ: multiply field, area and the perpendicular share.

For a curved surface or changing field, split the surface into small patches. Each area vector dA points along its chosen normal and has a size equal to the patch’s area. Add E·dA across the patches. Reversing the chosen normal reverses signed flux without changing the field.

lessons.title: Relate local outflow to total boundary flux
lessons.idea: Imagine a tiny closed box in a flow.
body: Imagine a tiny closed box in a flow. Compare how much goes out through its sides with how much comes in. Divergence is that net outward amount per tiny volume as the box becomes very small. Positive means more out than in; negative means more in than out. The same mathematical idea also applies to fields that are not fluids.

For a field F, add three matching rates: how its x part changes along x, its y part along y, and its z part along z. The result ∇·F is one number at each place. For F = (x,y,z) with dimensionless values, each matching rate is 1, so the divergence is 3.

The divergence theorem connects the inside and the boundary of a region. Adding divergence throughout its volume equals adding outward flux through the complete enclosing surface. dV is a tiny volume, while dA is a tiny area arrow pointing outward. The circle on ∮boundary marks the closed enclosing surface here.

A field can be nonzero and uniform without local net outflow.

apply.text: Why is a closed surface essential when applying a volume-to-boundary relation?
apply.answer: It must enclose the region whose internal divergence is being integrated. An arbitrary open patch is only part of a boundary and does not capture total outward flux.

lessons.limits: Singular sources require careful integral treatment or generalized functions. Do not apply smooth-field formulas blindly at a point charge.

lessons.title: Relate local circulation to boundary circulation
lessons.idea: Curl describes a field’s local tendency to circulate.
body: Curl describes a field’s local tendency to circulate. A tiny paddle wheel in a fluid can help you picture this turning tendency, but curl is not simply a test of whether drawn arrows look curved. The field need not be a fluid.

In the xy plane, compare two sideways rates: ∂Fᵧ/∂x − ∂Fₓ/∂y. This gives the z component of curl, written (∇×F)z. The notation ∇×F names the whole curl vector. Here +z points out of the page, toward you. A positive z component corresponds to a counterclockwise tendency as you view the page.

Stokes’s theorem joins the surface and its edge. Add curl through a surface, or add the field’s along-path contribution around its complete edge: the totals agree under the stated conditions. Choose the area normal with your right thumb; curled fingers set the matching direction around the edge. Reversing one orientation requires reversing the other.

The z curl is ∂x/∂x − ∂(−y)/∂y = 1 − (−1) = 2.
Around a counterclockwise unit circle, circulation is 2π, matching curl 2 times area π.

All coordinates and field values in this example are dimensionless. The other curl components are zero. The unit circle has radius 1 and area π; multiplying its area by the constant z curl 2 gives circulation 2π, with the matching counterclockwise direction.

apply.text: Why must the direction of a loop be specified when calculating circulation?
apply.answer: Reversing the traversal changes the line integral’s sign. The normal of the associated surface must reverse too for Stokes’s theorem to remain consistent.

lessons.title: Keep two components in one number
lessons.idea: A complex number keeps track of two parts together.
body: A complex number keeps track of two parts together. Write z = a + ib: a is its real part and b is its imaginary part. The number i is defined by i² = −1. “Imaginary” is a mathematical name, not a warning that the calculation is fake. On a number diagram, draw a across and b up.

The magnitude |z| is the distance from zero, found using √(a²+b²). The conjugate z* keeps a and reverses the sign of b. Multiplying z* by z gives a²+b², the squared distance. The star marks conjugation, while the centred dot means multiplication. The numbers here have no physical units.

Magnitude squared is not automatically a probability. In a suitable quantum calculation, amplitudes are complex numbers assigned to specified alternatives. They must obey the model’s normalization rule before their squared magnitudes can be used as probabilities. The physical rules come later.

lessons.title: Distinguish magnitude from angle
lessons.idea: Two complex numbers can have equal size but point in different directions on their number diagram.
body: Two complex numbers can have equal size but point in different directions on their number diagram. Their angle from the positive real direction is called phase. Relative phase is the difference between two such angles. It repeats after each full turn of 2π radians. Zero has no defined phase.

Adding complex numbers means adding their real parts and their imaginary parts separately. Equal values in the same direction reinforce: 1+1=2. Equal values in opposite directions cancel: 1+(−1)=0. Both inputs in the second sum have size 1, but their phases differ by π radians, half a turn.

In quantum theory, some alternatives have a meaningful relative phase and must be combined as amplitudes; these are called coherent alternatives. Where the physical model says to combine them, add amplitudes first, then take the squared magnitude. Which alternatives combine this way depends on the setup; this lesson does not decide that physical question.

Each has magnitude 2, but the sum is 2 + 2i.
The sum’s magnitude is √8, not 4. Their phases differ by π/2.

apply.title: Avoid a probability error
apply.text: Why can you not always add probabilities when two quantum alternatives interfere?
apply.answer: When the physical setup requires coherent alternatives, add their complex amplitudes first, then square the magnitude of that sum. Coherent means they have a meaningful relative phase in that setup. The sum can include interference effects, so adding the separate probabilities can give a different answer. lessons.title: Divide by clearing the imaginary denominator
lessons.idea: To divide by a nonzero complex number, multiply the top and bottom of the fraction by its conjugate.
body: To divide by a nonzero complex number, multiply the top and bottom of the fraction by its conjugate. Multiplying both by the same nonzero number leaves the fraction unchanged. The denominator then becomes real.

For denominator c+id, the conjugate is c−id. Their product is c²+d² because i²=−1. So the reciprocal is (c−id)/(c²+d²). The real numbers c and d cannot both be zero. For 1+i, the denominator product is (1+i)(1−i)=1−i²=2.

Our numerical examples have no units. If the original quantity has units, its reciprocal has reciprocal units. An angle of −π/4 means 45 degrees clockwise from the positive real direction. A very small denominator can make a result large and sensitive to small changes; do not hide that by rounding.

lessons.title: Separate size from phase
lessons.idea: Euler’s formula gives two descriptions of the same point on a circle in the complex-number diagram.
body: Euler’s formula gives two descriptions of the same point on a circle in the complex-number diagram. One uses cosine and sine; the other uses the exponential e raised to iθ. The number e is about 2.71828. The angle θ is in radians, and i²=−1.

In e^(iθ)=cos θ+i sin θ, cosine gives the horizontal part and sine the vertical part. This point always stays one unit from zero. A nonzero complex number can be written r e^(iθ), where r is its positive magnitude and θ its phase. At r=0 the value is zero and phase is undefined.

Multiplying by e^(iφ) rotates the diagram angle by φ without changing size. This is an abstract number rotation, not a claim that an object physically circles. For a real repeating signal, the real part of A e^(iωt) is A cos(ωt): A is real and has the signal’s units, ω is angular frequency, and t is time.

lessons.title: Differentiate a rotating phase factor
lessons.idea: For a steady repeating signal, complex notation can shorten rate calculations.
body: For a steady repeating signal, complex notation can shorten rate calculations. Write its complex form as X e^(iωt), with X a fixed complex amplitude and ω a fixed nonnegative angular frequency. A derivative with respect to time becomes multiplication by iω. Taking a second derivative multiplies again: (iω)²=−ω².

Each time derivative adds inverse seconds to the units. In the worked position example, taking real parts gives 2 m cos(3 t/s), velocity −6 m/s sin(3 t/s), and acceleration −18 m/s² cos(3 t/s). The tilde over x labels the complex calculation; measured position is its real part.

For the later application, x″ means acceleration, ω₀ is the positive natural angular frequency and f₀ is driving acceleration. A trial response gives (ω₀²−ω²)X=f₀ when ω differs from ω₀. This is one forced response, called a particular solution. A homogeneous solution solves the equation with the drive removed; it is generally also needed to match starting position and velocity. A transient is a starting-condition contribution, not part of the steady repeating response.

lessons.title: Recover the measurable real signal
lessons.idea: A complex number can help us calculate a real repeating signal.
body: A complex number can help us calculate a real repeating signal. At the end, take the real part: the component without i. Write the constant complex amplitude X=a+ib. Both a and b have the signal’s measured units.

Multiply a+ib by cos(ωt)+i sin(ωt). The real terms are a cos(ωt)−b sin(ωt); the minus sign comes from i×i=−1. The same signal can be written A cos(ωt+φ), where A=√(a²+b²) is its nonnegative amplitude and φ is the phase of X. If X=0, the signal vanishes and no phase is defined.

For X=(2+i) V, the signal starts at 2 volts but its peak magnitude is √5 volts. Starting value is not necessarily amplitude. Using a negative exponential instead is also possible, but all phase signs and derivative rules must use that same convention. Taking real parts works through addition and multiplication by real constants; do not assume it works through every nonlinear operation, such as squaring.

lessons.title: A matrix transforms components
lessons.idea: A matrix is a table of numbers that tells us how to combine inputs.
body: A matrix is a table of numbers that tells us how to combine inputs. Each row gives instructions for one output. For A=[[2,0],[0,1]], the first row means 2 times x plus 0 times y. The second means 0 times x plus 1 times y. Thus A(x,y)=(2 x,y). A names the matrix; x and y are inputs, not multiplication signs.

The main diagonal runs from top left to bottom right. Entries away from it are off-diagonal entries: they let one input affect a different output. Matrix dimensions mean row and column counts, not physical units. Our examples have no units. An inverse would undo the operation, but not every matrix has an inverse.

lessons.title: Keep transformation order explicit
lessons.idea: Doing two operations in a different order can change the answer.
body: Doing two operations in a different order can change the answer. Stretching an arrow and then turning it need not give the same result as turning it first. In ABv, start with v, apply B, then A. The grouping (AB)v=A(Bv) does not reverse this order.

In the example, S doubles the horizontal component and R rotates 90 degrees counterclockwise. Both are operations on dimensionless two-part vectors. RSv means stretch first, then rotate. SRv means rotate first, then stretch.

AB−BA is a matrix that compares the two orders on any input. If it is the zero matrix, the pair commutes: order makes no difference for every vector. Some pairs commute and some do not. Matrix sizes must allow each output to serve as the next input. In quantum theory this difference is called a commutator, with further physical meaning taught later.

lessons.title: Solve and verify a component system
lessons.idea: Sometimes we know an output and want to recover its input.
body: Sometimes we know an output and want to recover its input. In Av=b, the matrix A acts on the unknown vector v to give the required output vector b. If A has an inverse, that inverse undoes the operation and gives v=A⁻¹b.

For the two-by-two matrix [[a,b],[c,d]], calculate ad−bc, called the determinant. If it is nonzero, swap a and d, reverse the signs of b and c, then divide all four entries by ad−bc. This gives the inverse matrix, not entry-by-entry reciprocals. Here the scalar entry b and the output vector b in Av=b are different objects distinguished by context.

For a diagonal matrix with entries 2 and 4, the inverse has entries ½ and ¼. It changes output (6,8) back to input (3,2). All values here are unit-free. If the determinant is zero, the matrix is singular: it cannot be undone uniquely. Depending on the requested output, there may be no solution or many.

lessons.title: Change the description, not the vector
lessons.idea: A basis is a collection of vectors that describes every vector in a space in exactly one way.
body: A basis is a collection of vectors that describes every vector in a space in exactly one way. The basis spans the space: its combinations reach every vector. Its vectors are independent: none can be built from the others. The same physical arrow can have different component lists in different bases.

Put the new basis vectors into the columns of P, using their old coordinates. The list v_new says how much of each new basis vector to use. Multiplying P v_new reconstructs v_old. For an operation, read A_new=P⁻¹A_oldP from right to left: convert new coordinates to old, apply the old description, then convert back. Neither the vector nor the physical operation has changed.

In the swap example, e′₁ and e′₂ label the first and second new basis vectors; the prime means new, not a derivative. A perpendicular unit-length basis is orthonormal in real space. With a nonorthonormal basis, component dot-product rules require extra overlap information. In quantum descriptions, a basis state labels a specified alternative; a bare component list does not identify those alternatives.

lessons.title: Find directions a transformation preserves
lessons.idea: Some nonzero input vectors keep the same component pattern when a matrix acts: every component is multiplied by one common number.
body: Some nonzero input vectors keep the same component pattern when a matrix acts: every component is multiplied by one common number. These are eigenvectors. Av=λv says the output of A on v is λ times v. The number λ, said “lambda”, is the eigenvalue.

For real vectors and real λ, positive λ keeps direction, negative λ reverses it, and zero λ sends it to zero. The zero vector is excluded as an eigenvector because it satisfies the equation for every λ and identifies no special factor. Complex eigenvalues can require complex vectors; they are not simply stretches of real arrows.

Use A=[[2,0],[0,1]] in the worked example. In a connected oscillator system, a normal mode is a motion pattern whose coordinates keep fixed relative amounts. Eigenvectors can identify those patterns, but converting eigenvalues into frequencies requires the particular motion equation, not an arbitrary matrix.

lessons.title: Calculate the allowed scale factors
lessons.idea: To find eigenvalues, look for values of λ that permit a nonzero vector to obey Av=λv.
body: To find eigenvalues, look for values of λ that permit a nonzero vector to obey Av=λv. Rearranging gives (A−λI)v=0. I is the identity matrix: it leaves vectors unchanged. Subtracting λI subtracts λ from the diagonal entries of A.

The determinant, written det, tests whether this matrix can be undone uniquely. When det(A−λI)=0, a nonzero vector can map to zero, so λ can be an eigenvalue. For [[2,1],[1,2]], the determinant is (2−λ)(2−λ)−1×1. Setting it to zero gives (2−λ)²=1, so λ is 1 or 3.

Check each proposed eigenvector by multiplying A by it. A scalar is one number, whereas a matrix is a table. A singular matrix has no inverse. Repeated eigenvalues do not guarantee enough independent eigenvectors for a basis; additional properties are needed to guarantee real eigenvalues.

lessons.title: Choose coordinates adapted to an operator
lessons.idea: A matrix can be easier to use when we describe vectors with a basis of its eigenvectors.
body: A matrix can be easier to use when we describe vectors with a basis of its eigenvectors. In those coordinates, each component is multiplied separately rather than mixed with the others. This requires enough independent eigenvectors to form a full basis.

P has those eigenvectors as columns. D is diagonal: entries away from the main diagonal are zero, and its diagonal contains the matching eigenvalues in the same order. In A=PDP⁻¹, read right to left: convert to eigenvector coordinates, scale each component with D, then convert back.

Aⁿ means apply A a positive whole number n times. The conversions between successive applications cancel, leaving PDⁿP⁻¹. Raise each diagonal eigenvalue to n. Thus a factor 3 applied twice gives 9, not 6. The example matrices are dimensionless.

Two matrices commute when AB=BA. A Hermitian matrix equals its conjugate transpose: swap rows and columns and conjugate every entry. For finite-dimensional Hermitian matrices, commuting allows a common eigenvector basis. This special condition must not be assumed for arbitrary operations.

steps: Take A = [[2,1],[1,2]], whose eigenvectors (1,1) and (1,−1) have eigenvalues 3 and 1.

Matrix multiplication gives P⁻¹AP = [[3,0],[0,1]] = D. The diagonal order matches the eigenvector column order.
For u = (1,1), applying A twice gives 3²u = 9u. This follows directly from the diagonal action.

lessons.title: Compare states with an inner product
lessons.idea: An inner product compares two vectors and returns one number.
body: An inner product compares two vectors and returns one number. For real vectors in perpendicular unit coordinates, it is the dot product. For complex vectors in an orthonormal basis, conjugate each component of the first vector, multiply by the matching component of the second, then add.

The bracket ⟨u|v⟩ names this inner product. The norm ||v|| is a generalized length: the nonnegative square root of ⟨v|v⟩. Subscripts label components; a star means conjugate. Our examples are unit-free.

Orthogonal vectors have inner product zero. A normalized vector has norm 1. An orthonormal basis has norm 1 for each basis vector and zero inner products between different basis vectors. Dividing a nonzero vector by its norm normalizes it. For amplitudes (1,1), division by √2 makes the sum of squared magnitudes 1; unnormalized components are not already a complete probability distribution.

lessons.title: Separate size from direction
lessons.idea: Normalization keeps a nonzero vector’s pattern but changes its overall size so its norm is 1.
body: Normalization keeps a nonzero vector’s pattern but changes its overall size so its norm is 1. Divide every component by the same norm. A hat marks the resulting normalized vector: v̂=v/||v||.

For v=(1,i), conjugation gives (1,−i). Its squared norm is 1+(-i)i=2, because i²=−1. Its norm is √2, so the normalized components are 1/√2 and i/√2. Their squared magnitudes are ½ and ½ and add to 1. Dividing by 2 instead would use the squared norm, not the norm.

The inner product must be positive-definite: every nonzero vector has strictly positive squared norm. Zero cannot be normalized because division by zero is undefined. If listed squared amplitudes total less than 1, either normalization is missing or some alternatives are missing. Fixing the sum alone does not prove the physical model is valid.

lessons.idea: A projection asks how much of a vector lies along a chosen direction.
body: A projection asks how much of a vector lies along a chosen direction. In a real picture it resembles an arrow’s shadow along that direction. Let u be a unit vector, so ⟨u|u⟩=1. Calculate c=⟨u|v⟩, then multiply u by c. The coefficient c and the projected vector uc are different answers.

A complete orthonormal basis consists of mutually orthogonal unit vectors that reach every vector by combination. Only with such a complete basis does adding all squared projection-coefficient magnitudes recover the full squared norm. An incomplete set can miss part of the vector.

lessons.title: Turn a rate rule into an evolution
lessons.idea: A differential equation gives a rule for how something changes instead of giving its value directly.
body: A differential equation gives a rule for how something changes instead of giving its value directly. An ordinary differential equation, or ODE, uses derivatives with respect to one input, often time. For a nonnegative amount N, dN/dt=−kN says its rate of decrease is proportional to the amount remaining, with positive constant k.

N(t)=N₀e^(−kt) obeys this rule. N₀ is the starting amount at time zero, and e≈2.71828. Multiply k by time before applying the exponential; kt has no units. The same formula describes many starting amounts, so an initial value is needed to choose one.

In the example, 100 becomes about 36.8 in the same amount units after 5 seconds. This is a smooth model amount, not a claim that a single particle can be counted fractionally. To test the solution, check both its time derivative and its starting value.

apply.answer: Differentiate it: dN/dt = −kN₀e^(−kt) = −kN. Then check N(0) = N₀. Both the rate rule and initial condition must match.

lessons.limits: This first-order ODE needs one initial value. More complicated systems may need several initial/boundary conditions and numerical methods.

lessons.title: Use the initial value and time scale
lessons.idea: In exponential decay, the same fraction remains after each equal time interval.
body: In exponential decay, the same fraction remains after each equal time interval. If half remains each interval, the amounts go 100,50,25—not 100,50,0. This assumes the positive rate constant k stays fixed.

The characteristic time τ (tau) is 1/k. After this time about 36.8 percent remains, because e^(−1)≈0.368. The half-life t½ is the time until 50 percent remains. It equals ln 2 divided by k. The natural logarithm ln undoes the natural exponential: ln 2 is the power to which e must be raised to obtain 2, about 0.693.

If k is 0.1 per minute, the characteristic time is 10 minutes and the half-life is about 6.93 minutes. They answer different questions. A smooth average decay curve does not predict the exact time of each random individual event.

lessons.title: Solve a restoring-rate equation
lessons.idea: An ideal oscillator moves back and forth because its acceleration points toward its centre.
body: An ideal oscillator moves back and forth because its acceleration points toward its centre. Let x be displacement from that centre. The symbol x″ means the second time derivative of x: acceleration. The rule x″+ω₀²x=0 means acceleration is −ω₀² times displacement. Farther from the centre gives a stronger acceleration back toward it.

The positive natural angular frequency ω₀ measures phase change per second. A solution is x(t)=A cos(ω₀t)+B sin(ω₀t). Both A and B have length units. To determine them, specify starting position and velocity: A=x(0) and B=v(0)/ω₀. The zero in parentheses means evaluate at time zero.

With starting position 3 cm and starting velocity zero, the example begins at its positive extreme. Its initial acceleration is −12 cm/s², toward the centre. The model has no damping or drive and uses an acceleration proportional to displacement. Radians are required in these derivative formulas.

lessons.title: Separate transient and forced responses
lessons.idea: A pushed oscillator has three influences: a restoring effect toward its centre, damping that reduces motion, and an outside push that repeats.
body: A pushed oscillator has three influences: a restoring effect toward its centre, damping that reduces motion, and an outside push that repeats. In x″+2βx′+ω₀²x=f₀ cos(ωt), x is displacement, x′ is velocity and x″ is acceleration. The damping constant β is positive. The natural angular frequency ω₀ is positive; ω is the nonnegative drive angular frequency. The nonnegative driving acceleration size is f₀. Every term has acceleration units.

The full motion is a free response plus one driven response. Free, or homogeneous, means solving with the drive set to zero. Particular means one solution with the drive present. With positive damping the starting-condition contribution, called a transient, fades. The long-time response follows the drive frequency, though its phase—its place in the repeating cycle—can differ from the drive.

To calculate its steady amplitude A, square the frequency-mismatch term ω₀²−ω² and the damping term 2βω, add them, take the nonnegative square root, then divide f₀ by that result. A is the greatest displacement magnitude in that steady response, not displacement at the present instant. At zero damping and exact resonance there is no bounded steady sinusoidal solution; real-system limits cannot be ignored.

lessons.title: Treat linked quantities as a system
lessons.idea: Two connected oscillators can affect each other.
body: Two connected oscillators can affect each other. Collect their displacements into a column vector r. Its second time derivative r″ contains their accelerations. The matrix K stores the restoring effects after dividing out mass. Its entries have units per second squared, so −Kr has acceleration units.

A normal mode is a motion pattern that keeps its component proportions as its overall size changes. If Ku=λu with λ>0, this pattern obeys an oscillator equation with angular frequency √λ. The minus sign in r″=−Kr is essential: it makes the acceleration restoring. This frequency interpretation comes from this particular equation, not from any eigenvalue of any matrix.

For K=[[2,−1],[−1,2]]ωₛ², the pattern (1,1) moves both coordinates together and (1,−1) moves them oppositely. Their frequencies are ωₛ and √3 ωₛ. For example, if ωₛ=2 rad/s, these are 2 rad/s and √12 ≈ 3.46 rad/s. A full basis of independent modes lets us combine such patterns to describe general initial motion in this linear model.

lessons.title: Build a shape from simple waves
lessons.idea: A complicated repeating signal can be built by adding simple sine and cosine waves.
body: A complicated repeating signal can be built by adding simple sine and cosine waves. Each ingredient has a size and a repetition rate; together they shape the signal. They are mathematical ingredients, not necessarily separate physical objects.

The fundamental period T is the shortest positive time after which the whole signal repeats. The fundamental frequency f₀=1/T counts repeats per second, in hertz. Angular frequency ω₀=2π/T counts radians per second because one repeat has 2π radians. For T=2 s, these are 0.5 Hz and π rad/s.

Harmonics are whole-number multiples of the fundamental frequency. In the example we call the signal q(t), so its name is not confused with s for seconds. Its dimensionless value is sin[(2π s⁻¹)t]+0.3 sin[(6π s⁻¹)t]. The coefficients inside the angles are angular frequencies; multiplying by time makes dimensionless sine arguments. The two ingredients have frequencies 1 Hz and 3 Hz, and the second has 0.3 times the amplitude of the first. Nonrepeating signals can instead use a continuous-frequency description, called a Fourier transform.

lessons.title: Describe a nonperiodic wave packet
lessons.idea: A Fourier transform describes a signal by its repeating-wave ingredients instead of its values at each position.
body: A Fourier transform describes a signal by its repeating-wave ingredients instead of its values at each position. For a nonrepeating signal these ingredients can have a continuous range of wave numbers. Wave number k means phase change per metre, measured in radians per metre.

The original signal ψ(x), read “psi of x”, depends on position x. Its transform ψ̃(k), “psi tilde”, is a complex weight assigned to k. Multiply ψ(x) by e^(−ikx), continuously add over all x using the integral, then multiply by 1/√(2π). Here i²=−1, e≈2.71828, and dx is a small length contribution. The product kx has no units. With this convention the transform’s units are the signal’s units times length.

The worked box has height 1 and width 2 metres. At k=0 the rotating factor is 1, so only its area matters:2 metres divided by √(2π), about 0.798 metre. This weight is not a probability or a normalized quantum state. A matching inverse transform rebuilds the original signal; signs and factors must be used as a consistent pair.

An FFT, or fast Fourier transform, is a numerical algorithm for a finite sampled transform. Finite recording duration and sample spacing limit what it reveals. In the later quantum relation p=ℏk, p means momentum and ℏ is the reduced Planck constant in joule seconds. That relation needs quantum assumptions and well-defined variances; it is not a conclusion about every signal.

Therefore ψ̃(0)=2 m/√(2π) ≈ 0.798 m with this transform convention. The transform has length units because the input signal is dimensionless and dx has units m.

apply.text: Can a finite recorded signal determine arbitrarily fine frequency differences?

lessons.title: A density becomes a probability only after integration
lessons.idea: A probability tells how likely an outcome is.
body: A probability tells how likely an outcome is. For a continuous measurement described by a density, ask for the chance of landing inside a range. The height of the density graph alone is not that chance. The nonnegative density ρ(x), read “rho of x”, must integrate to 1 over all possible values.

P(a≤x≤b) means the probability that x lies between a and b. Integrating ρ(x) from a to b adds density across that interval. If x is in metres, density is per metre, so the product with dx gives unit-free probability. The density itself can exceed 1 in its units without making an interval probability exceed 1.

The mean or expectation ⟨x⟩ weights each value by its density and adds over all possible x. It has the same units as x and need not be an outcome of a single measurement. Variance is the average squared distance from the mean, with squared variable units. Some distributions do not have finite means or variances; these formulas require the relevant integrals to exist.

lessons.idea: One motion can answer different questions.
body: One motion can answer different questions. Position says where the object is. Velocity says how quickly position changes, including direction. Acceleration says how quickly velocity changes. Our ideal position signal is x(t)=(0.02 m)cos[(3 s⁻¹)t]: its amplitude is 2 centimetres and its phase changes at 3 radians per second.

Differentiate position once for velocity and twice for acceleration. Divide 2π by angular frequency for the time of one full repeat. Integrate velocity from starting time t₁ to finishing time t₂ for displacement: final position minus initial position, not final position by itself.

For this signal the period is about 2.094 seconds. Over one whole cycle the net displacement is zero because the object returns to its start, but total distance is four amplitudes,0.08 metre. At time zero the object is momentarily at rest at its positive extreme; its negative acceleration means it starts moving back toward the centre. The model assumes one frequency and no damping.
